slides.headline: Controlling jobs. In one sentence
slides.body: needs orders jobs and carries their results, if decides whether a job or step runs, timeout-minutes bounds how long it may run, and continue-on-error lets a failure pass without failing what contains it.

slides.headline: Matrix. In one sentence
slides.body: a matrix turns one job definition into one job per combination of the values you list, each with its own runner and its own matrix context.

slides.headline: Matrix. In one sentence
slides.body: strategy.matrix maps variable names to lists, and the jobs are the Cartesian product: every combination of one value from each list.

slides.headline: Matrix. In one sentence
slides.body: exclude removes combinations, and a partial match is enough.

slides.headline: Matrix. In one sentence
slides.body: include is processed after exclude.

slides.headline: Matrix. In one sentence
slides.body: fail-fast defaults to true: when one matrix job fails, the in-progress and queued ones are cancelled.

slides.headline: Matrix. In one sentence
slides.body: A run may generate at most 256 matrix jobs.

slides.headline: Matrix. In one sentence
slides.body: A job-level if is evaluated before the matrix is expanded, so it can't read matrix.

slides.headline: Matrix. In one sentence
slides.body: And outputs of matrix jobs are merged into one set, and the last writer wins, in no guaranteed order.

slides.headline: Artifacts. In one sentence
slides.body: an artifact is a set of files that a job uploads to GitHub, where it's stored with the run, can be downloaded by later jobs or by people, and expires after a retention period.

scoped to the job: downloadable by a later job of the same run as soon as the upload step ends

slides.direction: The root-cause box of section 20A.11, one line at a time. Observed behavior: a dependency was upgraded, CI still installs the old version from cache. Mechanism: the key had no lock-file hash, or a broad restore key matched an old entry, which was then extended and saved under the new key. Root cause: caches are immutable per key and restore keys match by prefix. Correct fix: put `hashFiles` of the lock file in the key; install from the lock file, with `uv sync --locked`, so that a stale cache cannot change what is installed. Prevention: a manual prefix, such as `v2-`, to invalidate everything at once.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : a dependency was upgraded, CI still installs the old version from cache
Mechanism         : the key had no lock-file hash, or a broad restore key matched an old entry,
                    which was then extended and saved under the new key
Root cause        : caches are immutable per key and restore keys match by prefix
Correct fix       : put hashFiles of the lock file in the key; install from the lock file
                    (uv sync --locked) so that a stale cache cannot change what is installed
Prevention        : a manual prefix (v2-) to invalidate everything at once

slides.headline: Now Lab 26.8 on your practice repository, in your normal shell
slides.body: The interface changes. The lab text and the linked documentation are the reference, and no GitHub output was captured by the authors.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: A cache key without the lock file's hash, or with a broad restore key. Root cause: caches are immutable per key and restore keys match by prefix, so an old entry keeps being restored.
Rebuilding in the deploy job. Root cause: a second build resolves dependencies again, so the deployed files are not the tested files; pass the build as an artifact.
An if on a job that is a required check. Root cause: a job skipped by its if reports success for its check.
No timeout-minutes. Root cause: the default of 360 minutes is also the hard limit for a GitHub-hosted job, so a hanging test bills six hours.
Requiring the individual matrix jobs in a ruleset. Root cause: their set and names change when the matrix changes; require one aggregate job with a fixed name.

beats.text: Two complaints, and no bug in GitHub. CI is the automated testing that runs on each change, and a dependency is a package your project needs. The first complaint is a cache doing exactly what a cache is defined to do. The second is a team that rebuilt in the deploy job what it had already built and tested in another job. They got a different result, because the dependencies resolved again.
beats.tele: Two complaints, and no bug in GitHub. CI is the automated testing that runs on each change, and a dependency is a package your project needs. The first complaint is a cache doing exactly what a cache is defined to do. The second is a team that rebuilt in the deploy job what it had already built and tested in another job. They got a different result, because the dependencies resolved again.

beats.text: Both come from using a cache or an artifact without knowing what each one promises. A cache promises nothing: it may be absent. An artifact promises that the bytes you download are the bytes that were uploaded. This video gives you both definitions, and the rules for ordering and multiplying jobs that you need before either matters. Keep the first complaint in mind. Why would CI keep installing the old version?

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. In GitHub Actions, a workflow is a file that says: when this event happens, run these jobs. A job is a list of steps that run in order on one fresh machine, the runner. You can now read a trigger, an expression and a shell invocation, and you know what the checkout leaves on the runner. This video is about the structure above the steps: how jobs relate to each other.

A job is a list of steps that run in order on one fresh machine, the runner. You can now read a trigger, an expression and a shell invocation, and you know what the checkout leaves on the runner. This video is about the structure above the steps: how jobs relate to each other.

beats.text: Four topics, in the order of sections 20A.9 to 20A.12. Controlling jobs with needs, if, timeout-minutes and continue-on-error, including two rules about skipping that decide whether a pull request can merge. A pull request is GitHub's proposal to merge one branch into another. Matrix strategies, and how to count the jobs of a matrix. Dependency caching: keys, restore order, scope, eviction and trust. And artifacts: what crosses from one job to the next as files.

And artifacts: what crosses from one job to the next as files.

beats.text: Controlling jobs. In one sentence: needs orders jobs and carries their results, if decides whether a job or step runs, timeout-minutes bounds how long it may run, and continue-on-error lets a failure pass without failing what contains it.
beats.tele: Controlling jobs. In one sentence: `needs` orders jobs and carries their results, `if` decides whether a job or step runs, `timeout-minutes` bounds how long it may run, and `continue-on-error` lets a failure pass without failing what contains it.

beats.text: needs, at job level: the job waits for the listed jobs. If one of them fails or is skipped, this job is skipped, unless its if says otherwise. Without needs, jobs run in parallel.
beats.tele: `needs`, at job level: the job waits for the listed jobs. If one of them fails or is skipped, this job is skipped, unless its `if` says otherwise. Without `needs`, jobs run in parallel.

beats.text: if, at job or step level: the job or step runs when the expression is truthy, meaning it counts as true. An expression is a formula that GitHub Actions replaces with its value. An if without a status function behaves as if success() and a logical "and" were in front of it. So the default is success().
beats.tele: `if`, at job or step level: the job or step runs when the expression is truthy, meaning it counts as true. An expression is a formula that GitHub Actions replaces with its value. An `if` without a status function behaves as if `success()` and a logical "and" were in front of it. So the default is `success()`.

beats.text: timeout-minutes: the job or step is cancelled after that many minutes. The default for a job is 360.
beats.tele: `timeout-minutes`: the job or step is cancelled after that many minutes. The default for a job is 360.

beats.text: continue-on-error: a failure doesn't fail the job, at step level, or the run, at job level.
beats.tele: `continue-on-error`: a failure doesn't fail the job, at step level, or the run, at job level.

beats.text: The status functions change the implicit success(). failure() is true when an earlier step or needed job failed. always() is true even when the run was cancelled. cancelled() is true on cancellation. The expressions page advises against always() for anything that could fail critically and recommends !cancelled() for "run whether or not the earlier steps passed". You saw that form in the lint workflow.
beats.tele: The status functions change the implicit `success()`. `failure()` is true when an earlier step or needed job failed. `always()` is true even when the run was cancelled. `cancelled()` is true on cancellation. The expressions page advises against `always()` for anything that could fail critically and recommends `!cancelled()` for "run whether or not the earlier steps passed". You saw that form in the lint workflow.

beats.text: continue-on-error at step level splits a step's result in two. The outcome is the result before the setting is applied. The conclusion is the result after. A failed step with the setting has outcome failure and conclusion success.
beats.tele: `continue-on-error` at step level splits a step's result in two. The `outcome` is the result before the setting is applied. The `conclusion` is the result after. A failed step with the setting has outcome `failure` and conclusion `success`.

beats.text: Quick quiz. A required check is a check that a rule says must pass before a pull request can merge. Suppose that job gets skipped by its own if. Does the check A, block the pull request, or B, count as passed? Your answer?

beats.text: Matrix. In one sentence: a matrix turns one job definition into one job per combination of the values you list, each with its own runner and its own matrix context.
beats.tele: Matrix. In one sentence: a matrix turns one job definition into one job per combination of the values you list, each with its own runner and its own `matrix` context.

beats.text: strategy.matrix maps variable names to lists, and the jobs are the Cartesian product: every combination of one value from each list. Then:

beats.text: exclude removes combinations, and a partial match is enough.

beats.text: include is processed after exclude. An entry is added to every existing combination it can extend without overwriting an original matrix value. If it would overwrite one, it becomes a new combination of its own.

beats.text: A job-level if is evaluated before the matrix is expanded, so it can't read matrix.

beats.text: And outputs of matrix jobs are merged into one set, and the last writer wins, in no guaranteed order.

beats.text: Caching. In one sentence: a cache stores a directory under a key so that a later run with the same key can restore it and skip the download. It's an optimization that may be absent, never a place to keep something you need.
beats.tele: Caching. In one sentence: a cache stores a directory under a key so that a later run with the same key can restore it and skip the download. It's an optimization that may be absent, never a place to keep something you need.

beats.text: The key: at most 512 characters, usually built from the operating system and hashFiles of a lock file. A lock file pins each dependency to one exact version, and a hash is a fingerprint computed from content. An existing key is never overwritten. The documentation: "You cannot change the contents of an existing cache."

A lock file pins each dependency to one exact version, and a hash is a fingerprint computed from content. An existing key is never overwritten. The documentation: "You cannot change the contents of an existing cache."

beats.text: The restore order. First the exact key. Then entries whose key starts with the key. Then each restore-keys prefix in order, the most recently created match winning.
beats.tele: The restore order. First the exact key. Then entries whose key starts with the key. Then each `restore-keys` prefix in order, the most recently created match winning.

beats.text: Saving: on a miss, the cache is saved at the end of the job, and only if the job completes successfully.
beats.tele: Saving: on a miss, the cache is saved at the end of the job, and only if the job completes successfully.

beats.text: The cache-hit output: true only for an exact match on the primary key. False when a restore key matched, or nothing was restored.

beats.text: Scope: a run can restore caches created on its own branch or on the default branch. A pull request run can also restore from its base branch. Sibling branches can't read each other's caches. A cache saved by a pull request run belongs to the merge ref, GitHub's test merge of that pull request, and is restorable only by re-runs of that pull request.
beats.tele: Scope: a run can restore caches created on its own branch or on the default branch. A pull request run can also restore from its base branch. Sibling branches can't read each other's caches. A cache saved by a pull request run belongs to the merge ref, GitHub's test merge of that pull request, and is restorable only by re-runs of that pull request.

beats.text: Eviction: entries not accessed for seven days are removed. A repository gets ten gigabytes without charge. Above the limit the least recently used entries are deleted. Administrators can raise the limit, billed, since the twentieth of November 2025.
beats.tele: Eviction: entries not accessed for seven days are removed. A repository gets ten gigabytes without charge. Above the limit the least recently used entries are deleted. Administrators can raise the limit, billed, since the twentieth of November 2025.

beats.text: Trust: anyone who can open a pull request can read caches of the base branch, and cache contents aren't signed. Since the twenty-sixth of June 2026, events that people without write access can cause get a read-only token for the default branch's caches. And since the tenth of September 2026 the cache-mode key states the access explicitly, with the values read, write, write-only and none. Cache poisoning is a topic of Part 7.
beats.tele: Trust: anyone who can open a pull request can read caches of the base branch, and cache contents aren't signed. Since the twenty-sixth of June 2026, events that people without write access can cause get a read-only token for the default branch's caches. And since the tenth of September 2026 the `cache-mode` key states the access explicitly, with the values `read`, `write`, `write-only` and `none`. Cache poisoning is a topic of Part 7.

beats.text: Most projects never write a cache block, because the setup actions, packaged steps, contain it. actions/setup-java with cache: maven stores the Maven repository under a key that hashes the POM files by default. astral-sh/setup-uv has enable-cache with the default auto: enabled on GitHub-hosted runners except for release, tag push, pull_request_target and workflow_run events.

beats.text: Artifacts. In one sentence: an artifact is a set of files that a job uploads to GitHub, where it's stored with the run, can be downloaded by later jobs or by people, and expires after a retention period.
beats.tele: Artifacts. In one sentence: an artifact is a set of files that a job uploads to GitHub, where it's stored with the run, can be downloaded by later jobs or by people, and expires after a retention period.

beats.text: Immutability: an artifact can't be changed after upload. A second upload with the same name in one run fails unless overwrite is true.
beats.tele: Immutability: an artifact can't be changed after upload. A second upload with the same name in one run fails unless `overwrite` is true.

beats.text: Availability: downloadable by a later job of the same run as soon as the upload step ends.
beats.tele: Availability: downloadable by a later job of the same run as soon as the upload step ends.

beats.text: Retention: 90 days by default. retention-days goes from 1 to 90, never above the repository or organization setting. Since the first of October 2026 the same setting also deletes checks, workflow runs and commit statuses.
beats.tele: Retention: 90 days by default. `retention-days` goes from 1 to 90, never above the repository or organization setting. Since the first of October 2026 the same setting also deletes checks, workflow runs and commit statuses.

beats.text: Limits: 500 artifacts per job. Hidden files are excluded unless you include them explicitly.
beats.tele: Limits: 500 artifacts per job. Hidden files are excluded unless you include them explicitly.

beats.text: Permissions: zipped uploads don't keep file permissions. If the executable bit matters, tar the files first.
beats.tele: Permissions: zipped uploads don't keep file permissions. If the executable bit matters, tar the files first.

beats.text: Outputs: an artifact ID, a URL, and a SHA-256 digest, a fingerprint of the uploaded bytes.
beats.tele: Outputs: an artifact ID, a URL, and a SHA-256 digest, a fingerprint of the uploaded bytes.

beats.text: Download: by name into a path. Version 8 fails on a digest mismatch by default.

beats.text: Analogy, from the textbook. A cache is the shared fridge at work with labelled boxes. If a box with your label is there, lunch is quick. If it was cleared out, you cook again. You don't keep your passport in it, and you don't eat from a box whose label you didn't write.

beats.text: The textbook says where it holds and where it breaks. It holds for eviction and for trust. It breaks on mutability, because a cache entry can never be changed once saved. The fridge box can be refilled. A cache key can't.

beats.text: That immutability is the mechanism behind the first complaint from the opening. If the key doesn't change when the dependencies change, the old box keeps being found.

beats.text: Then the documentation's rule for choosing between the two: a cache for files that are reused between runs and can be recreated, such as dependencies. An artifact for files a job produced that must be passed to another job or kept after the run, such as build outputs and test reports.
beats.tele: Then the documentation's rule for choosing between the two: a cache for files that are reused between runs and can be recreated, such as dependencies. An artifact for files a job produced that must be passed to another job or kept after the run, such as build outputs and test reports.

beats.text: And the reason behind that rule, which the textbook sets in bold: the files that were tested are the files that are deployed. A rebuild in a second job resolves dependencies again, possibly to different versions.
beats.tele: And the reason behind that rule, which the textbook sets in bold: the files that were tested are the files that are deployed. A rebuild in a second job resolves dependencies again, possibly to different versions.

beats.text: So when you see data moving between jobs, ask: is this something I could lose without consequence? Then it's a cache. Is this the thing itself? Then it's an artifact.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: A cache key without the lock file's hash, or with a broad restore key. Root cause: caches are immutable per key and restore keys match by prefix, so an old entry keeps being restored.
beats.tele: A cache key without the lock file's hash, or with a broad restore key. Root cause: caches are immutable per key and restore keys match by prefix, so an old entry keeps being restored.

beats.text: Rebuilding in the deploy job. Root cause: a second build resolves dependencies again, so the deployed files are not the tested files; pass the build as an artifact.
beats.tele: Rebuilding in the deploy job. Root cause: a second build resolves dependencies again, so the deployed files are not the tested files; pass the build as an artifact.

beats.text: An if on a job that is a required check. Root cause: a job skipped by its if reports success for its check.
beats.tele: An `if` on a job that is a required check. Root cause: a job skipped by its `if` reports success for its check.

beats.text: No timeout-minutes. Root cause: the default of 360 minutes is also the hard limit for a GitHub-hosted job, so a hanging test bills six hours.
beats.tele: No `timeout-minutes`. Root cause: the default of 360 minutes is also the hard limit for a GitHub-hosted job, so a hanging test bills six hours.

beats.text: Requiring the individual matrix jobs in a ruleset. Root cause: their set and names change when the matrix changes; require one aggregate job with a fixed name.
beats.tele: Requiring the individual matrix jobs in a ruleset. Root cause: their set and names change when the matrix changes; require one aggregate job with a fixed name.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. The textbook's instruction for an ML team: cache package downloads and small test models, never multi-gigabyte checkpoints.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. The textbook's instruction for an ML team: cache package downloads and small test models, never multi-gigabyte checkpoints.

beats.text: Here's how that goes wrong. A team that evaluates language models caches a model checkpoint of several gigabytes "to make the evaluation job faster". It works. A week later every other job in the repository is slow. The ten gigabytes per repository are shared by all branches, the checkpoint filled most of them, and above the limit the least recently used entries are deleted. The model cache evicted the dependency caches that made CI fast.
beats.tele: Here's how that goes wrong. A team that evaluates language models caches a model checkpoint of several gigabytes "to make the evaluation job faster". It works. A week later every other job in the repository is slow. The ten gigabytes per repository are shared by all branches, the checkpoint filled most of them, and above the limit the least recently used entries are deleted. The model cache evicted the dependency caches that made CI fast.

beats.text: The decision is the one from the mental model. Can the checkpoint be lost without consequence? It can be downloaded again, so it's cache material in principle, but its size makes it the wrong tenant for a shared ten gigabytes. And for upload of reports from that evaluation, the textbook adds two rules.

beats.text: Upload test reports with if: failure() and a short retention. And never upload a directory that may contain credential files or a .git folder with persisted credentials, because an artifact is a copy of those files that outlives the job.
